title: "HumanKind Global"
url: "https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/case/humankind-global"
date: "2021-02-19"
summary: "Volunteers fulfill more than 25,000 requests for pandemic-related help"
source: "The GovLab (virtual-communities.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# HumanKind Global

**Volunteers fulfill more than 25,000 requests for pandemic-related help**

- Founding year: 2020
- Group size: 51500
- Location: India
- Part of: [The Power of Virtual Communities](https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/)

## Introduction

When India went into a nationwide lockdown in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, restrictions on movement affected how people across the country could access medicine, food and other supplies that they needed on a daily basis. As people with compromised immune systems are at particularly high risk, many people living with HIV/AIDS feared traveling to clinics and labs to pick up medication. Needing help, some turned to HumanKind Global, a network of thousands of volunteers across India and other countries who coordinate mutual aid via a Facebook group and several groups on WhatsApp. HumanKind Global volunteers delivered HIV medication to more than 170 people across India during those first four weeks.

HumanKind Global (previously known as Caremongers India) was created in March 2020 by 39-year old Mahita Nagaraj, a self-employed digital marketing professional and single mother based in Bangalore. In six months, the group has grown to more than 50,000 members who have fulfilled more than 25,000 requests for help across India and 14 other countries.[1] "In a time of fear, anxiety and panic, we should spread love and care to those who are struggling," Nagaraj [told The Straits Times](https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/south-asia/coronavirus-over-22000-caremongers-help-vulnerable-and-elderly-indians-under).

## How it All Started

In mid-March, as the number of coronavirus cases in India rose, Mahita Nagaraj [began to receive](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-india-52045544) requests for help from friends who lived overseas, asking if she could deliver medicine and food to their elderly parents around Bangalore. Realizing that many in the city were in high-risk groups due to either their age or pre-existing health conditions, Nagaraj posted on Facebook an offer to deliver necessary supplies to anyone in the city who needed help. She was met with a flood of responses; for every one person requesting assistance, several more were asking Nagaraj how they could help.

Needing a structured way to coordinate this growing volunteer network, Nagaraj created a Facebook group, originally known as Caremongers India, on March 17, 2020. The group’s original name was inspired by a [BBC article](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-51915723) about “Caremongering,” a trend where people on Facebook in cities across Canada set up mutual aid communities to spread kindness and support as an antidote to “scaremongering” about the coronavirus. Nagaraj changed the group’s name to HumanKind Global in February of 2021.

Since many elderly Indians were not on Facebook, Nagarj also set up a WhatsApp line that those in need could call or text to request help. “At one point in time we were adding 2,000 to 3,000 members a day to the Facebook group, and the helpline was exploding,” Nagaraj told us. “We were receiving 800 to 1,000 calls a day and 2,500 WhatsApp messages.” She attributes this rapid growth to the high demand for help among vulnerable populations during India’s coronavirus lockdown, which was among the strictest in the world. Many elderly Indians also depend on external help, such as chauffeurs, public transit and delivery services, which were unavailable throughout much of the lockdown.

## Leadership

The size of the group’s leadership team has fluctuated along with the group’s growth. At one point, it had as many as a dozen moderators, but as of August 2020 the group was run by Nagaraj along with two other admins and one moderator. This “core team” (as Nagaraj describes the quartet) is responsible for moderating membership and approving and tagging posts, as well as matching volunteers to requests that come in through the helpline. When Nagaraj noticed volunteers who were particularly active, she invited them to take on leadership roles as coordinators for certain cities or areas. “As the group grew, their roles grew in size and form, from being just city coordinators to being part of the team that headed states, or that helped disseminate information, to then being part of the core team,” Nagaraj explains.

Those in need can request help anonymously by calling or texting a WhatsApp number, which Nagaraj and the core team operate. Depending on where the requester is located, the team may then push the request to one of several WhatsApp groups, composed of volunteers in cities across India, or post the request to the Facebook group. People can also post requests directly to the Facebook group. Nagaraj says that requesters typically find a volunteer to help them within 30 seconds of posting to the group.

Nagaraj set up seven rules for the Facebook group, which prohibit hate speech and bullying, advertising, spam, and fundraising, and encourage members to be kind and courteous. Nagaraj says that members’ behavior in the group has not been a major issue, and that this simple set of rules has been enough to keep things civil.

## Participation

The group is public and visible, meaning that anyone can find it, read its posts, and request membership. While primarily active in India, the group has members from 100 countries and has run requests in 14 other countries.

On the “supply” side, people volunteer their time and skills. The accessibility of the public Facebook group provides a low barrier to entry - all someone needs to do in order to join as a volunteer is send a post or message making themself available. Nagaraj estimates there are 8,000 to 10,000 volunteers who are actively running requests for those in need.

On the “demand” side, Nagaraj says HumanKind Global primarily caters to four vulnerable populations that:

- Are older than 60
- Have pre-existing medical conditions
- Have physical disabilities
- Are pregnant women or new mothers

## Action

HumanKind Global has delivered groceries and medicine, and organized blood donations and nursing assistance, among many other requests it has answered. Nagaraj says the nature of requests has evolved; while early on there was a high demand for medical assistance or people asking to be driven to their doctor’s appointment, as India’s lockdown has been rolled back, the group has fulfilled more requests for information, for instance, about travel restrictions.

In addition to fielding ad hoc requests, HumanKind Global has also streamlined the request matching process by compiling a database of people in need. Anyone who anticipated needing help during India’s extended lockdown could register their name in the database online. A team of 50 - 60 HumanKind Global volunteers then contacted each of the 2,500 registrants to ask their location and what type of assistance they may need over the next one or two weeks. Nagaraj says this “citizens’ database” helped registrants to feel more secure, “since they knew they were being looked after,” and helped HumanKind Global streamline their response during the country’s lockdown, since they could more effectively plan how to allocate resources.

## Outcome and Impact

Of the more than 25,000 requests fulfilled by HumanKind Global volunteers, several actions stand out as particularly impactful.

A couple in the southern state of Kerala was in need of medication for their seven month-old infant, who suffered from epileptic seizures, but they were unable to find the medicine anywhere near them during the lockdown. Knowing that their child could face lifelong chronic health effects if they did not receive the medication within 72 hours, the couple reached out to HumanKind Global via the WhatsApp helpline. Volunteers delivered the medication from the state of Maharashtra (some 1,000 km away) with two hours to spare. HumanKind Global was able to coordinate this feat during a time when non-essential travel was not permitted and medicine was in short supply.

In another case, a 74-year old man returned to his apartment complex in Kolkata after spending six months visiting family in Australia. Despite completing the mandatory quarantine, the building’s security guards were still fearful that the man might be carrying coronavirus and could transmit it to others, and locked him inside his nearly-empty apartment. The man contacted the HumanKind Global helpline, and a volunteer brought him food, water, and his medication. “The volunteer only left the premises after he got an assurance from one of the neighbors that they would look after this gentleman and make sure that he was well looked-after,” Nagaraj says.

## Challenges

Keeping up with the pace of growth has been a challenge for the group, which gained several thousand members in its first week, and continued to grow rapidly throughout the lockdown. Nagaraj says that she spent up to 22 hours per day coordinating requests during the lockdown, which she did on an unpaid, volunteer basis. While membership is no longer growing as rapidly, she says she “didn’t have a moment to breathe” from the group’s founding in March, until the end of July 2020.

One operational challenge has been deciding which requests the group should and should not fulfill. Nagaraj says that India’s government has set up its own programs to assist people dealing with coronavirus-related issues and that HumanKind Global has to be mindful that the help they provide does not take people away from these official channels. For instance, the group does not coordinate blood donation for those seeking plasma therapy as a treatment for COVID-19, since such treatment is regulated by the government.

Some have also tried to take advantage of the group’s kindness to request help when they don’t need it. For example, Nagaraj says that around a fifth of the requests the group has received are from healthy people who just don’t feel like leaving home. “I would get requests from people who wanted me to bring them butter chicken and pizza and tacos,” Nagaraj explains. “They were healthy citizens who simply didn’t want to go out and put themselves at risk.” Nagaraj says that after a couple of these bogus requests, she began contacting requesters over the phone and asking screening questions to make sure they really needed help before dispatching a volunteer.

When asked about operating on Facebook or WhatsApp,  Nagaraj did not raise any concerns. Rather, she says that as a completely volunteer-run project, HumanKind Global depends on free tools from Facebook and WhatsApp to carry out its work.

## Future Prospects

Nagaraj wants to transform HumanKind Global into a community that continues to help people after the pandemic. She hopes that registering the group as a nonprofit will help the community to continue to expand beyond India. “The nature of activity will remain the same, which is that we will be a volunteer-driven organization, but one that exists internationally and not just locally,” Nagaraj explains.

## Lessons learned

- **Be willing to adapt -** Nagaraj says that part of the group’s strength is its ability to adapt as the nature of requests changes. “Our philosophy at the beginning was that help would be offered to those who asked for it,” she explains. “The nature of help, to this day, remains completely undefined. If you need something done, you come forward and ask for it, and we’ll find a way to make sure it gets done.” In a context where travel restrictions and public health guidance can change by the hour, if not the minute, this flexibility to adapt has never been more valuable.
- **More than just a trend -** While the popularity of “caremongering,” and kindness-first, mutual aid communities has grown since the pandemic began, HumanKind Global stands out for its real-world impact at scale. It is an organized, volunteer-led crisis response platform that provides substantive help to those most in need. “We formed as a community in response to a pandemic, a certain environmental situation,” Nagaraj says. “I think one of the strengths of the group has been our ability to respond as required to whatever the situation has thrown at us.”

## End notes

1. As of October 2020

date: "2021-02-23"
summary: "500,000 women are finding empowerment through entrepreneurship"

# Clube da Alice

**500,000 women are finding empowerment through entrepreneurship**

- Founding year: 2014
- Group size: 551,500 members (Private Group)
- Location: Curitiba, Brazil
- Part of: [The Power of Virtual Communities](https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/)

## Introduction

In spring 2017, a collaborative creation space called the Clube da Alice Lounge opened at the Mueller Shopping complex in Curitiba, a city of 1.8 million people in southern Brazil. The Lounge provides a physical space for nearly three dozen female entrepreneurs to showcase and sell their products to customers in the large mall. These entrepreneurs and small business owners are members of the Clube da Alice Facebook group, a broader networking community and marketplace for female entrepreneurs across the Curitiba region. The Lounge is just one of many resources the group has created in order to serve Curitiba’s local entrepreneur community.

Clube da Alice was founded in 2014 by Brazilian entrepreneur Mônica Balestieri Berlitz. According to the [Clube da Alice website](https://www.clubedaalice.com.br/newsletter/), Berlitz created the group “to promote female entrepreneurship through a free channel for publications of products / services, in addition to encouraging the debate of issues related to the universe of women.”[1] Today, the group has more than 500,000 members who make 3,000 posts daily, making Clube da Alice [one of the most prominent](https://www.assespropr.org.br/mulheres-na-t-i-conheca-a-historia-de-monica-berlitz-fundadora-do-clube-da-alice/) Facebook groups in Latin America.[2] The group provides these members, many of whom are independent creators with limited resources, with access to a large, trusted network of potential clients and partners.

## How it All Started

In 2014, Berlitz was looking for a way to publicize a fashion magazine called Palpite da Alice (“Alice’s Guess”), of which she was the editor. Berlitz began to promote the publication on Facebook, and was met with an outpouring of support and positive feedback from other members of the female online entrepreneur community. This experience [gave Berlitz the idea](https://www.assespropr.org.br/mulheres-na-t-i-conheca-a-historia-de-monica-berlitz-fundadora-do-clube-da-alice/) “to create a safe environment for women to advertise their businesses” as well as “facilities and transparency for those who wanted to purchase their products.”[3]

Berlitz [named the new community](https://revistaviver.com.br/?p=27009) Clube da Alice in homage to Lewis Caroll’s book, Alice in Wonderland. As Berlitz told us in a recent interview, the group is meant for women who, like the girl who fell through the looking glass, are friendly, ethical, and respectful of differences, yet also questioning, critical, and curious.

## Leadership

![Clube Da Alice Berlitz Headshot](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/b0eca7bf-bdc7-4c20-a172-207df23b4869.jpg)

*Figure 1: Mônica Berlitz created Clube da Alice in 2014 to provide female entrepreneurs with a safe environment to showcase their products and build connections. Photo courtesy of Mônica Berlitz.*

Berlitz, who is Clube da Alice’s sole [administrator (admin)](https://www.facebook.com/help/901690736606156), is supported by a team of approximately a dozen [moderators](https://www.facebook.com/help/901690736606156). Berlitz looks for group members who exhibit empathy for others and who she feels are engaged in the community, understand it well, and know how to use the tools of the Facebook platform. Berlitz says that at one time, the group had a professional moderation team on payroll, but she found that volunteers were more effective moderators because they truly cared about the community and its values. The group raises money through profits from products that use the Club’s brand, sponsorships with other brands, paid events, and paid memberships. Those who sign up for a paid club [membership](http://carteirinha.clubedaalice.com.br/) can access exclusive events and discounts on products and services with partnering businesses around Curitiba.

Governance is extensive. Moderators enforce more than [50 rules](https://www.clubedaalice.com.br/regras-do-clube-da-alice/), many of which derive from Brazilian law, which are designed to create a safe, ethical, and legal marketplace for women to sell their products within the Facebook group. The group developed many of these rules in coordination with regulatory authorities in response to particular issues. For instance, Berlitz says that some group members wanted to sell homemade cheeses, which can be illegal and unsafe, so they created a rule that any cheese products sold on the group must be certified by a local regulatory authority.

Clube da Alice also worked with the Brazilian agency that oversees trademarks and intellectual property to ensure that posts follow national intellectual property laws. Other rules outlaw posts that promote multi-level marketing (“pyramid schemes”), sweepstakes and raffles, religious posts, sharing “controversial” publications, and fake profiles. These rules are a result of the unique space that the Clube da Alice Facebook group occupies as both an online community and a marketplace for the sale of digital and physical products.

## Participation

Clube da Alice is composed primarily of female business owners and professionals in the Curitiba metropolitan area. Berlitz says that “Alices,” as members of the group are colloquially known, fall into three categories:

1. Entrepreneurs - women who advertise their businesses and products
2. Consumers - women who come to the group to buy goods and services
3. Observers - women who are in the group for entertainment or to conduct market research but do not actively participate.

Women join because the group provides them a platform to make professional and personal connections with other participating community members and to showcase their products in a virtual space. Berlitz says that women feel more comfortable conducting business within the closed community than they would buying or selling on another online platform. The group provides members with access to this large platform as well as information about how to price their products and sustainably operate their businesses.

Clube da Alice is a “secret” group, meaning that new members must be invited to join by a current member. Any invitee who identifies as female is eligible to join. New members may find out about the group through several channels outside Facebook, including a [newsletter](https://www.clubedaalice.com.br/newsletter/), [blog](https://www.clubedaalice.com.br/blog/), and [Instagram page](https://www.instagram.com/clubedaalice/?hl=en).

## Action

Clube da Alice is primarily an online network to build business connections and sell goods and services, from beauty and fashion services to handicrafts to food. The community includes everything from doctors offering consultations to vendors selling seasonal produce. A [2020 article](https://www.brazilianjournals.com/index.php/BRJD/article/view/12063/10083) published by the Brazilian Journal of Development describes Clube da Alice as a “large collaborative network” to which entrepreneurs come to sell products and consumers come in order to learn about new sellers and to exchange information, for instance, about the quality of products.[4] Enabling local commerce through online transactions is particularly important during the COVID-19 pandemic when in-person commerce has stalled. Berlitz says participation has substantially increased since the pandemic began.

Members also form personal connections. Berlitz tells of a member who learned that she had developed breast cancer at a young age. When her doctor told her that getting more exercise would improve the effectiveness of her chemotherapy treatment, the young woman turned to Clube da Alice to find other people to accompany her on daily walks. More than 200 women joined up. Berlitz says that with the community’s support, this member has not only beaten breast cancer but gone on to run marathons.

To build this sense of community, the leadership team engages with members both on the secret group and the public [Facebook page](https://www.facebook.com/clubedaaliceoficial/). Berlitz often hosts livestreams with guests who speak about a range of topics, from makeup tutorials, to the experience of Black women in the tech entrepreneur community, to the role of women in politics.

## Outcome and Impact

According to Berlitz, the group’s greatest impact is its ability to facilitate business connections that help female entrepreneurs to succeed. For instance, Berlitz says that one young woman began posting about the traditional Brazillian desserts that she was baking at home. The desserts were a hit, and the woman was able to expand her small business from an at-home operation to three pastry shops that employs 30 people. “It wasn’t Clube da Alice that did this, but rather the connections she formed within the group,” Berltiz told us.

Berlitz says that these stories of empowerment underscore the growing role of women in the Brazilian labor market, which goes far beyond simply making money. “We think about entrepreneurship only while generating income, but it can also help women to see themselves differently within the family,” [she told](https://www.jornale.com.br/post/2020/06/27/Clube-da-Alice-passa-a-fazer-parte-do-Shopping-Crystal) the Curitiba-based news site Jornale. She says the economic independence that women build through entrepreneurship can also translate to greater autonomy in their roles as providers for their family.[5]

## Challenges

As a large group, moderating the huge volume of posts and comments can be a challenge. Berlitz says that the Facebook algorithm can be inconsistent and will sometimes incorrectly flag posts as violating the platforms rules. The original poster then wrongfully accuses the moderation team of removing their post. Berlitz says there has been an uptick in these sorts of contentious interactions since the pandemic began, since the group is much more active in the absence of in-person opportunities to sell products.

When asked about operating Clube da Alice on a private platform, Berlitz did not raise any major concerns. Rather, she says that the group has to respect Facebook’s rules and that she spends a lot of time working with the moderators to make sure they understand the platform’s rules and how to use its tools to enforce them.

Berlitz does say that Facebook’s moderation tools could be improved. For instance, it can be difficult for moderators to make announcements since their post may not show up on all members’ feeds. She would like to see improvements in how moderators’ announcements and posts are distributed to group members.

## Future Prospects

Berlitz’s goal for the future is to reach and impact as many women as possible. Clube da Alice [is participating](https://www.facebook.com/community/2020communitydirectory/) in the 2020 [Community Accelerator](https://www.facebook.com/community/2020communitydirectory/), a Facebook-led program that provides training, mentorship, and funding to help online communities grow. She hopes to expand the group beyond the Curitiba region to other cities in Brazil.

The group is also continuing to expand the array of services it offers to members. Clube da Alice is working with the Curitiba city government to connect women with free education programs about finance and technology for business. In addition to the Clube da Alice Lounge, the group [is developing](https://www.jornale.com.br/post/2020/06/27/Clube-da-Alice-passa-a-fazer-parte-do-Shopping-Crystal) a “collaborative creation space” at the Shopping Crystal mall in Curitiba. The 115 m² retail space will consist of two storefronts, one of which will include a recording studio, which is intended as resources for members to use to create and sell their products. In another example, in 2020 the group worked with the [Tipay app](https://tipay.app/) (a Brazil-based mobile payment platform) to launch [AlicePay](http://www.clubedaalice.com.br/alicepay/#home), a mobile application for processing digital payments. In both these cases, Clube da Alice worked with an outside company to develop products tailored to group members while also strengthening the Clube da Alice brand.

## Lessons learned

- **Intimacy by design -** A sense of community is what sets Clube da Alice apart from other run-of-the-mill online marketplaces and sell-and-swap shops. *Alice in Wonderland*\-themed imagery, such as white rabbits and skeleton keys, features prominently on the group’s website, giving the “club” a fantasy-inspired feeling of secrecy and intimacy. Berlitz sees the sense of belonging as key to fostering positive interactions between members: “Often when people react aggressively in the group, it's because they don't feel like they belong, in some way, to what is being created,” she says. “But once people feel like they belong to a community, they work to nurture connections with one another.”
- **Rules grounded in experience -** Clube da Alice’s collection of rules is extensive and extremely specific. Since the group developed many of the rules with legal or professional authorities on specific issues, the rules have an aura of legitimacy. The consistent and effective enforcement of the rules is key to maintaining the safe and transparent marketplace that the group’s vendors and sellers rely upon.

## End notes

1. Quote translated by Google
2. As of October 23, 2020
3. Quote translated by Google and edited for clarity
4. Translated by Google
5. Translated by Google and edited for clarity.

title: "Essex Coronavirus Action"
url: "https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/case/essex-coronavirus-action"
date: "2021-02-23"
summary: "Mobilizing Essex residents and Facebook group leaders for coronavirus response"
source: "The GovLab (virtual-communities.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# Essex Coronavirus Action

**Mobilizing Essex residents and Facebook group leaders for coronavirus response**

- Founding year: 2020
- Group size: 37,000 members (private group); 48,000 followers (public page)
- Location: Essex, United Kingdom
- Part of: [The Power of Virtual Communities](https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/)

## Introduction

When Olivia (a pseudonym) was discharged from the hospital in early 2020, the 92-year old woman was worried about how she would cope with the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. Through Facebook, Olivia connected with  Essex County Council (ECC), the local government authority that oversees a county of 1.5 million people in southeastern England. ECC connected Olivia with [United in Kind](https://www.facebook.com/unitedinkind), a volunteer network that ECC, along with hundreds of community groups, charities, volunteer organizations, and leaders of Facebook groups across the county, coordinates via a Facebook page. United in Kind volunteers delivered food to Olivia’s home, drove her to medical appointments, and provided any other essential services that she required during the pandemic.

United in Kind is one of several resources that ECC has developed over the past two years as part of its new model of outreach to vulnerable populations. In addition to pushing out information about public services through traditional media channels, ECC decided to partner with local area Facebook groups and community organizations to reach a broader and more diverse audience. While this approach has led ECC and partners to develop a number of interesting projects, from anti-bullying campaigns to community fridges to recycling initiatives, the focus of this case study is on how ECC leveraged this unique partnership to respond to the pandemic through the Essex Coronavirus Action initiative.

## How it All Started

When Kirsty O’Callaghan joined ECC as its Head of Strengthening Communities in 2017, she was tasked with making public services more accessible to the county’s most vulnerable populations, including the elderly, socially isolated people, and those living in economically deprived areas. As the inspiration for turning to Facebook, O’Callaghan recalls an incident when her dog, Martha, escaped while she was away from home. She posted a plea for help to her local area Facebook group. “When I got home an hour later, there were 500 people out looking for Martha,” O’Callaghan remembers.

O’Callaghan realized that the leaders of these placed-based Facebook groups had both a deep knowledge of the problems facing their communities and the ability to reach people who may feel disconnected from local government. In 2018, she began asking local area groups in Essex whether they would be willing to collaborate with ECC on initiatives to address mental health problems that affected many parts of the county. Group leaders were quick to sign up, and the collaboration eventually spawned two mutual aid communities: [United in Kind](https://www.facebook.com/unitedinkind), for people suffering from social isolation and loneliness, and [Never Too Late, Mate](https://www.facebook.com/groups/nevertoolatematesupport), a male suicide prevention support group. In the two years since, the collaboration has grown into a network of 600 admins with a combined reach of more than 250,000 people.

When coronavirus began to spread across the United Kingdom in March of 2020, ECC mobilized this network to create a more organized and inclusive response. It created the public-facing [Essex Coronavirus Action](https://www.facebook.com/essexcoronavirusaction) page to disseminate Essex-specific information about public health guidance, pandemic-related public services, and volunteer opportunities. The Council also created a closed Facebook group, [Essex Coronavirus Action Support](https://www.facebook.com/groups/essexcoronavirusactionsupport), for citizens who wanted to privately ask questions and ask for help.

## Leadership

The Essex Coronavirus Action initiative is led by Essex County Council, The Essex Public Health Team, and the leaders of local area Facebook groups.

The private group is governed by a team of 18 admins. Three of these admins carry most of the workload and ECC pays them for their work. O’Callaghan said that the cost to the Council of paying these three admins had been about £70,000 over the first six months of the pandemic.

The admin team is led by community leadership consultant, Emmy Coffey McCarthy. McCarthy says that they have not set written rules for the group because they had to rapidly set it up and onboard members when the pandemic began. “We did not have time to do the usual niceties of declining with feedback and letting people know why their post wasn't acceptable,” McCarthy explains. Rather, the group deals with issues like misinformation on a case by case basis. The admins engage with people who share false information, correct them in a non-judgemental way and point them towards factual information that the group has posted. If necessary, members who continue to escalate arguments are banned or muted (meaning that they are unable to post or comment).

McCarthy says that interactions in the group tend to be civil and the admins rarely have to take punitive actions against members. “My admin team are very experienced and excellent communicators,” McCarthy says, “In 10 years of building digital communities, I have never run a group that relies so little on the tools available and so much on the personalities and skills of the active admins.”

## Participation

The Essex Coronavirus Action initiative targets county residents who use Facebook as a means of making connections and obtaining information. The private group has nearly 37,000 members, of which 20,000 joined within 72 hours of its creation. The admins ask people to provide their postal code when they request membership to verify that they live in Essex. The group is about 80 percent female and 20 percent male, although McCarthy says that men tend to be overrepresented in discussions. The group is not actively recruiting members, as they rely on the public page, which more than 48,000 users follow, to distribute information to the community.

O’Callaghan thinks that participation in the initiative has been higher than in a typical government program because the Council has reached far more people through Facebook than they could through traditional means. People are drawn to Essex Coronavirus Action’s identity as a collaborative effort rather than a top-down imposition from the government. “We brand very little as the Essex County Council, since people don’t like that brand,” O’Callaghan explains. “But they’ll trust this United In Kind thing because it looks accessible and like it’s not a local authority at all.”

## Action

The coronavirus response work in Essex is carried out through a combination of actions on the Page and private group, as well as volunteer-led actions in the real world.

The Essex Coronavirus Action Facebook Page distributes up-to-date information about the pandemic, including public health guidance and information for businesses who are reopening. For instance, in October 2020 the page posted a recording of a coronavirus press conference that was live streamed by the Prime Minister’s office. Such posts reached an estimated 2.1 million News Feeds during the first six weeks of the page’s existence. ECC continues to use the page to push out important information, which O'Callaghan says reaches up to 5 million people every month. ECC also posts information about resources for issues ranging from substance abuse to domestic violence to food insecurity.

The Essex Coronavirus Action Support group has a similar focus to the page, but creates more of a two-way conversation between members and admins. Members ask questions about testing, contact tracing, social distancing, travel restrictions and other pandemic-related topics, which admins or other members answer. Common topics of discussion are what behavior is allowed or advisable under current restrictions (e.g. “Is it safe to meet a family member at their home if we are outside?”, or “Do I have to wear a mask when I’m at the pub, even while seated at a table?”). Emmy McCarthy, or another admin, usually answers these questions and directs the member to relevant public health information.

ECC also uses its online presence to recruit volunteers to support the coronavirus response effort. Individuals and businesses can sign up via a form, which ECC promotes on the Facebook page as well as the [Essex.gov.uk](https://www.essex.gov.uk/community-support/volunteer-to-help-in-your-community) website. The form asks about the skills, qualifications, and type of support that volunteers are able to provide. Those who complete the form are entered into a database that ECC can draw on when someone requests assistance.

## Outcome and Impact

Between March 14 and March 21, more than 7,000 volunteers signed up to support the coronavirus response effort. Almost 2,000 individuals and more than 70 businesses registered within the first 24 hours. Every day this volunteer force completed more than 1,000 tasks, such as delivering essential supplies to people who were self-isolating and transporting vulnerable people to medical appointments. In one case one young woman returned home after giving birth to a new baby. However, she was not allowed to visit the hospital to breastfeed her baby (who had not yet been discharged) due to the pandemic. She reached out to ECC for help, and was connected with a volunteer who delivered breastmilk to the hospital everyday for months. O’Callaghan says using Facebook as a vehicle to advertise these volunteer opportunities has helped to engage people who want to help, but otherwise wouldn’t know how to get involved. Two-thirds of the volunteers ECC has engaged had no volunteering experience prior to the coronavirus relief effort.

ECC’s online presence has also helped to connect those in need with existing public services. In one case, a woman who lived in another county and was worried about how her elderly parents living Essex would cope during lockdown contacted ECC on Facebook. ECC was able to connect the woman’s parents with the county welfare service to make sure they were taken care of. O’Callaghan sees the Facebook-based outreach model as key to making these success stories a reality. “If we didn’t have this model, it wouldn’t have happened,” O’Callaghan explains. “Other counties have welfare services, and have it advertised in the local press, but they didn’t have the Facebook outreach model that went with it.”

While ECC does not have hard data about the impact of Essex Coronavirus Action on coronavirus spread or mortality rates, O’Callaghan says that the initiative has been a valuable tool to spread public health information, coordinate volunteer work, and identify the areas of the county that are most in need of government support.

## Future Prospects and Challenges

In addition to continuing their COVID-19 response work, ECC intends to turn their collaboration with Facebook into a model for public service delivery that other jurisdictions can replicate. The interest that other local government authorities in the UK have shown in Essex’s work inspired O’Callaghan to create a “community campaign model,” which explains how to build a group, map resources and partnerships, and recruit and train volunteers. ECC is working with Facebook and the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR), the government agency that oversees clinical research in the UK, to evaluate the model. The NIHR will evaluate the group’s work according to its impact, the connectivity of the team, and its use of Facebook tools among many other criteria.

O’Callaghan acknowledges the risk that Essex County Council’s work with Facebook may not continue in its current form if someday she is no longer there to support it. “I’ve had other team members say to me, ‘If you left the Essex County Council, this kind of work would die,’” O’Callaghan says. ECC's collaboration with Facebook groups depends on the political will of the Council’s leadership to continue to support the initiative. Local government authorities that want to replicate Essex’s success would need to find organizational leaders who are willing to take a chance on a partnership between the public and private sector as well as skilled and passionate public servants. As such, the transferability of ECC’s model to other jurisdictions remains to be seen.

## Lessons learned

- **Make participation accessible** - The ECC has pioneered new approaches to outreach and information dissemination. To counter fake news, the Essex Coronavirus Action group partnered with Simon Harris, who runs a popular [satirical news site](https://southendnewsnetwork.net/) in the UK, to develop engaging content that spreads factual information about the pandemic. “Simon is a genius at creating content and we work together really quickly,” O’Callaghan explains. “We write in a language that people can understand.” In another case, the group paid a popular reality TV star to record a [30-second video](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=3358770860812860) telling people in Essex to wear masks and practice social distancing. Strategies like these, as well as the streamlined process to register volunteers, has helped the ECC to engage populations who are typically disconnected from local government,
- **Be ready for action -** The Essex Coronavirus Action group was able to come together rapidly when the pandemic arrived because the needed infrastructure and institutional knowledge were already in place. Through existing projects like United in Kind and Never Too Late, Mate, the ECC and its Facebook group partners had experience in rapidly developing and launching public outreach campaigns based around Facebook Pages. As these initiatives also dealt with very personal public health issues (social isolation and male suicide, respectively) there was a local population who was familiar with and receptive to this form of outreach.
- **Blend online and offline** - By meeting people where they are, namely online, the local government is able to serve residents more effectively. Far from being divorced from geography, the Essex Coronavirus Action uses digital resources to help people in the local community. O’Callaghan feels that this blending of online and offline communities has changed, for the better, the way that the ECC operates. “I think every public sector organization in the world needs to work like this,” O’Callaghan says.

## End notes

NULL

type: "GovLab case study"
title: "Subtle Asian Traits"
url: "https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/case/subtle-asian-traits"
date: "2021-02-23"
summary: "1.8 million Asians living around the world connecting over a common identity"
source: "The GovLab (virtual-communities.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
---

# Subtle Asian Traits

**1.8 million Asians living around the world connecting over a common identity**

- Founding year: 2018
- Group size: 1843194
- Location: Global
- Part of: [The Power of Virtual Communities](https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/)

## Introduction

On July 9, 2020, a university student logged into Facebook and posted a photo of her grandfather showing off a massive winter melon that he had grown in the backyard. “Please drop cute photos of your family’s members with their fruit of labor,” she wrote.

Members of the Subtle Asian Traits Facebook group rose to the occasion and flooded the post with photos of their own family members holding yams, melons, and other fruits and vegetables they had grown. As Subtle Asian Traits co-founder Tony Xie explains, “Asians like to grow their vegetables and trees, and also take very cute pictures with them, holding them like a little prized baby. We’ve seen really wholesome threads of many other people doing the same thing.”

Xie, a 19 year-old based in Melbourne, was part of a group of nine Chinese-Australian high school students who created Subtle Asian Traits (SAT) as a place to share memes and jokes about their experience as first and second generation immigrants growing up in non-Asian cultures. SAT grew quickly as the group’s sense of humor caught on with young people of Asian descent around the world. Two years since its founding, the group has grown to more than 1.8 million members.[1]

## How it All Started

The Subtle Asian Traits Facebook group was created in September 2018 by a group of friends who had spent weekends together at Chinese language school. According to the group’s website, the founders saw a “gap in the internet for a place where all Asians could personally share their shared experiences in a light-hearted format without judgement.”[2] The name is a reference to Subtle Private School Traits, a [now-defunct Facebook Group](https://junkee.com/subtle-private-school-traits/175541) where students and ex-students shared memes about their experiences attending Australian private schools.

By December 2018, the group had gained more than a million members, as well as coverage by media outlets including the *New York Times*, BBC, *The Atlantic*, and *The New Yorker* magazine. This rapid growth made SAT’s founders realize they needed to put a goal down in writing: “Our mission is to connect Asian individuals globally to create a community that celebrates the similarities and differences within the subtle traits of Asian culture and subcultures.”

Tony Xie says that the group’s content resonates with young people of Asian descent, who often struggle to find others who share their experience at school or in other in-person communities. It allows them to create a majority Asian cultural community for people living in the Asian diaspora. As the online group took off, Xie and the other moderators were “amazed that there were just so  many people that could all have had a kind of similar experience growing up.”

## Leadership

![Sat Tonyxie (2)](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/57b46cc0-70a2-4f43-95ab-a5af1600de7c.jpg)

*Figure 1: Tony Xie co-founded Subtle Asian Traits in 2018. Photo courtesy of Tony Xie.*

The group of nine who created SAT are now in their teens and early twenties. They continue to lead the group along with 45 [admins and moderators](https://www.facebook.com/help/901690736606156) who manage SAT.

Tony Xie was a 17-year old high school student when he co-founded Subtle Asian Traits. Xie now admins the group while also pursuing a bachelor of science at the University of Melbourne. Zoe Imansjah, a chemical engineering student at the University of California, Santa Barbara, was not involved in the group’s founding, but was added to the group by a friend two months in and eventually became an admin.

![Sat Zoe Headshot](https://thegovlab-files.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/thegovlab-directus9/uploads/aaa54535-ed78-4568-821b-33b2d2dad63f.jpeg)

*Figure 2: University student Zoe Imansjah is part of SAT’s leadership team. Photo courtesy of Zoe Imansjah.*

As membership expanded, the admin team chose the most active members who they felt had a genuine interest in helping to run the community as moderators. Imansjah says the group avoided recruiting moderators who they felt just wanted to be involved with the group for “[clout](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/archive/2019/12/clout-definition-meme-influencers-social-capital-youtube/603895/),” namely to advance their own status on social media. Some moderators were chosen through an open application process, while the leadership team invited others to join them.

Subtle Asian Traits disallows spam and promotions, reposts, or unoriginal, off-topic or low-quality content in an effort to encourage high-quality postings. Even with a team of 45, approving each post is a significant workload for the moderation team. At times, up to 48,000 posts, many of which are repeats of the same meme or joke, have been in the queue awaiting approval. “There have been instances where I have literally spent the entire day just deleting the same post link over and over again after letting one through,” Imansjah told us. To deal with the volume of post requests, the moderation team must decide whether to accept or reject a post in only a few seconds. They also issue automated responses to explain to members why their posts were not approved. Facebook also worked with SAT to test a “bulk action” tool (which allows moderators to decline multiple post requests at once and provide pre-written feedback about why the posts were rejected), which the company says had helped the group to significantly reduce the amount of time the group’s moderators need to spend processing posts.

To prevent harassment, the group does not allow posts that target individuals. For instance, a post encouraging members to [dox](https://theconversation.com/what-is-doxxing-and-why-is-it-so-scary-95848) someone (meaning to release a person's personally-identifying information) would not be allowed, even if the person was thought to be racist or otherwise hostile to the community. “We don’t want to be fighting hate with hate,” Xie told us. “Nobody deserves to have 1.8 million people gang up on you.”

## Participation and Action

The 1.8 million-member group continues to grow rapidly, adding more than 10,000 members from September - October 2020. Members are mainly people in their teens and twenties who share the experience of living in a Western country as a person of Asian descent. According to the [BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-australia-46394931), posts “often focus on Asian culture as experienced by the children of migrants. That's why most members are young people from Australia, the US, Canada and the UK, rather than those living in Asia.”

Members participate because the group provides a shared sense of identity and experience.  In an [article for SupChina.com](https://supchina.com/2019/03/29/subtle-asian-traits-facebook-group-rallying-asians/), journalist Lavinia Liang interviewed co-founder Anne Gu about this shared sense of identity:

> “When the number of Americans in the group first surpassed the number of Australians, there was ‘a bit of a rivalry,” Gu said. But the group has since transcended that. “We’re not Asian Australians or Americans, we’re all just Asians in a big Westernized society, all merged into one category. We have the same names, the same traditions, the same struggles,” she said.

Members turn these experiences into posts and memes, which helps members to feel connected over cultural touch points like food, language, and family. In a 2018 [*New York Times* article](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/11/world/australia/subtle-asian-traits-facebook-group.html), Isabella Kwai writes that members share jokes “about the traits, subtle or otherwise, that characterize … the Asian-Australian experience, from cultural clashes with parents and the sanctity of bubble milk tea, to the groan-worthy pickup lines from white men on dating apps. (Are you from Asia? Because I’m China get your number.)” Posts like these continue to make up the bulk of the content shared to the group on a daily basis.

In the past, local chapters of the group also met offline to hold events such as trivia parties and meet-ups. In-person meetings have largely been put on hold due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

## Outcome and Impact

In addition to its value as a source of entertainment, Subtle Asian Traits seems to help many young Asian people feel more comfortable with their own identities and heritage in non-Asian cultures. “I think the page has really brought to light the fact that we first-second generation Asians are not alone in the way that we have grown up in a white society,” explains co-founder Lydia Jiang in [an interview with Vice](https://www.vice.com/en/article/d3nexw/subtle-asian-traits-holds-up-a-mirror-for-asian-australians-like-me). Likewise, in the *New York Times*, Isabella Kwai [writes](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/12/11/world/australia/subtle-asian-traits-facebook-group.html) that, “The endless stream of memes in the ‘Subtle Asian Traits’ group provides relief — it’s a chance to belong for once without having to try.”

Tony Xie sees the vegetable picture sharing case as an example of how the group facilitates connections over common cultural experiences. “It was really nice to see the whole community go bond over that little thing which, if you posted it in another place, might not generate the same reaction,” Xie told us. "There are a lot of really wholesome and lighthearted posts, but our group also has come to be a place where people share stories about challenges they face balancing Asian and Western cultures.”

In this vein, Subtle Asian Traits has also inspired many [unaffiliated spin-off groups](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/culture-desk/the-story-of-the-subtle-asian-traits-facebook-group) tailored to other identities, such as Subtle Asian Mental Health, Subtle Queer Asian Christian Traits, Subtle Asian Fitness, Subtle Curry Traits (for members of the South Asian community), and many others. Many of these spin-off communities provide a space for members not of East Asian descent, whom some [critics argue](https://mashable.com/article/subtle-asian-traits-meme-facebook-group/) are not well-represented in SAT.

## Challenges

Subtle Asian Traits faced significant challenges responding to the influx of political content across Facebook Groups that followed the police killing of George Floyd in May 2020, which also coincided with a resurgence of pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong.

The moderation team held an emergency three-hour meeting to discuss their approach for handling political discussion, a topic which was not previously allowed in the group. “As a community with quite a significant  influence we knew that we definitely had to say something about what was happening, and be a resource on what we could do,” Zoe Imansjah tells us, referring to the Black Lives Matter protests in the US. The moderators had to balance this sense of necessity with the risk of driving away members who used the group for respite and would be turned away by potentially polarizing content.

The moderators decided to post a megathread (a central thread for long discussions about a single topic) to aggregate discussions and resources about BLM. Xie and Imansjah say that it was a very stressful time for the moderation team, as they worked to verify every post to the megathread to avoid spreading fake news, and to combat harassment. “There was a mob mentality, where one person would say something and others would just pile on,” Xie explains. Some members criticized the group for “silencing” those who felt their comments were being buried in the megathread. SAT eventually began allowing a few discussion posts for each topic to keep the discussion reasonably centralized. “That decision kind of set a precedent to how we would handle future situations like this,” Xie says.

When asked about the unpaid time they invest leading Subtle Asian Traits, the admins say that, even though they spend a lot of time contributing to the group and driving users to the Facebook platform, they have a good relationship with the company and are willing to continue working on a volunteer basis. “I'm definitely one of  those people that likes to create communities, even if it's with my own time, if I feel that I'm contributing to something that is greater than myself,” Imansjah says.

## Future Prospects

Subtle Asian Traits is making an effort to become more inclusive for non-East Asian members of the community, such as people of South Asian descent. According to an [article](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-australia-46394931) published by the BBC, group co-founder Anne Gu says the administrators have since prioritised including more diverse content. Likewise, Imansjah and Xie report that the group is attempting to increase the diversity of its moderation and membership, in terms of ethnicity as well as factors such as occupation and age. “It's important to have those external viewpoints to make sure that we are respectfully addressing certain topics,” Imansjah says.

The group is also looking into backup platforms to use if someday they are no longer able to operate on Facebook, whose rules afford the company the unilateral right to terminate a group. “The worst case scenario would be if Facebook just decided to shut our group down, because maybe the discussions got way too heated,” Xie says. “That’s terrifying for us because if we lose our group, we lose almost two years of content, of stories of our community members;  it's like a little piece of history that just gets wiped away.” As such, the group is looking into blogging platforms and other social media platforms such as Instagram (which is also owned by Facebook) to keep the community together in case their group is shut down.

## Lessons learned

- **The right tool for the job** - Facebook is designed to share and provoke a discussion around multimedia content, making it well-suited to the kinds of content that Subtle Asian Traits produces. Kat Lin, in a [profile of SAT](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/culture-desk/the-story-of-the-subtle-asian-traits-facebook-group) published by *The New Yorker*, writes that “The format of the Facebook group promotes a digital solidarity: as posts explode with likes and comments, members individually tag close friends in the comments to alert them to the post. This means that a member can also see other peripheral friends or acquaintances … who are tagging their own close friends.” In other words, the Facebook groups platform is built to share relatable memes that will generate a reaction, and the Subtle Asian Traits group fully uses this functionality to its advantage.
- **Learning to walk the line -** Xie and Imansjah say that the group has faced a substantial amount of criticism related to diversity and the group’s response to discussions around the Black Lives Matter movement. They say that the leadership team sometimes feels invisible and attacked at the same time. Moderators have had to learn through experience how to respond to moments of crisis, and to do so while balancing their own opinions with those held by the wider community. “On one hand we do want to seem like we are real people, because that’s how you create a community,” Imansjah explains, “but on the other hand that opens us up to a lot of criticism from people saying that we're imposing our own principles and our own political views.” At the same time, the admins recognize that, as leaders of such a vast community, the decisions they make hold a great deal of influence. “As Uncle Ben in Spider-Man said, ‘with great power comes great responsibility,’” Imansjah says. “One wrong step and chaos breaks loose.”
- **Bonding over their outsider status** - Like many other successful groups on Facebook, Subtle Asian Traits brings together young people growing up Asian in non-Asian countries. The group unifies people who share a common cultural background and upbringing and affords them a place to express interest in their heritage, becoming part of a majority-Asian community despite growing up as the minority. The choice to create such a cross-cutting group, which couldn’t exist in the real world, creates an incentive for admins and moderators to volunteer their time and for members to join.

## End notes

1. As of October 2020

2. https://www.subtleasiantraits.com/index.html

date: "2021-02-23"
summary: "More than 900,000 women are supporting one another to overcome hardship"

licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"

# Surviving Hijab

**More than 900,000 women are supporting one another to overcome hardship**

- Founding year: 2014
- Group size: 917, 828 members of the private group
- Location: Egypt
- Part of: [The Power of Virtual Communities](https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/)

## Introduction

On March 25, 2019, a group of 14 women raised a banner reading “Surviving Hijab” over Mount Everest base camp.[1] The women who made the [eight-day trek](https://www.thenational.ae/uae/women-climb-to-everest-base-camp-to-show-unity-in-face-of-anti-hijab-rhetoric-1.848657) up the mountain’s south face were members of the Surviving Hijab Facebook group, a community created by Manal Rostom, a 40-year old Egyptian online influencer, marathon runner, and freelancer who is based in Dubai.

Rostom is a trainer and brand ambassador for Nike, and is also widely known for [testing and modelling](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/08/fashion/nike-pro-hijab-muslim-athlete.html) Nike’s “Pro Hijab,” a headscarf designed for athletic use.  She created Surviving Hijab in 2014 to provide a safe space for women to discuss their experiences being a woman in a Muslim culture and choosing to don the hijab. The group’s [purpose](https://www.facebook.com/groups/631337350298622/) is to “urge those who are veiled (and those who are considering in these hard times) to continue to hold on…despite the hardships.” Rostom led the Everest expedition to bring greater attention to the group’s mission: “What I wanted to achieve was to raise awareness about tolerance, inclusivity and equality for women,” [she told the Emerati daily](https://www.thenational.ae/uae/women-climb-to-everest-base-camp-to-show-unity-in-face-of-anti-hijab-rhetoric-1.848657), *The National*.

## How it All Started

As Rostom says, every woman who wears the hijab has a personal motivation - a “why” that reminds them of their faith. Rostom’s “why” came in 1999, when she was 19 years old. While on the way to a summer vacation at the Red Sea, the bus Rostom and her family were riding on blew a tire and crashed. Her cousin, with whom Rostom had switched seats only a few minutes earlier, was paralyzed and died a few months later. Miraculously, Rostom was unharmed. Feeling blessed by God, she decided to put on the hijab and has worn it ever since.

Rostom [created Surviving Hijab](https://darpanmagazine.com/people/newsmakers/manal-rostom-the-surviving-hijab-story/#:~:text=Later%20in%202018%2C%20Rostom%20won,efficiently%20through%20the%20required%20resources.) in 2014 as a community for women who wear the hijab to support one another through the personal, political and societal struggles that come with wearing the veil. An additional goal was to bring visibility to Muslim women, who Rostom says still face discrimination in both the Muslim and non-Muslim world. The rules of some sports leagues, for instance, do not allow athletes to wear the hijab during competition, forcing them to choose between their faith and sport. “We all have a voice - we just need to feel empowered to use it,” Rostom told us.

## Leadership

Surviving Hijab is run by a team of 10 [admins and moderators](https://www.facebook.com/help/901690736606156), most of whom are young women in the United Kingdom and Egypt. Moderators have to speak Arabic and English and be willing to put in the work - moderators spend up to six hours a day on the group encouraging the nearly 1 million members to post and engage with one another and enforce the rules of the group. Per the group’s rules, members are not allowed to tell another woman that her manner of dressing is not hijab. No bullying, “extremism,” re-posts, or off-topic posts are allowed. To protect members’ privacy, members are not allowed to share others’ posts outside the group.

Rostom interviews the candidates for a moderator position to make sure they are not religious extremists and have a genuine interest in the community, which is pro-hijab and embraces both religious identity and social integration.

Surviving Hijab is a forum for support. Women ask each other for advice and support as they consider wearing the hijab or when they struggle wearing it. In one recent post, a woman who was considering removing her hijab posted veiled and unveiled photos of herself and asked for others to pray for her. The post received over 13,000 [reactions](https://medium.com/facebook-design/reactions-not-everything-in-life-is-likable-5c403de72a3f) and over 3,000 comments - some encouraging her to wear the hijab, others in favor of removing it - within hours of its upload.

Fashion is another popular topic. When sorted by topic, “Fashion” and “Styling” represent the majority of tagged posts. These posts include a picture of a member’s outfit and ask for feedback, often with a variation of “What do you think?” as the caption. At the time of writing, members are participating in a challenge where a woman posts a picture of a princess alongside a photo of herself wearing the princess's outfit, usually adapted to include a headscarf. The picture challenges seem to be designed to emphasize that a woman can be whoever she wants to be in a hijab and that making an outfit out of it should be fun.

Women also ask for modesty tips, such as recommendations for wrist coverings. Beyond fashion, members celebrate important milestones within the group. Frequently, posts are about users’ birthdays, engagements and weddings, or anniversaries of their time wearing the hijab.

## Participation

As of October 2020, Surviving Hijab has more than 900,000 members, with more than 30,000 members added from September - October 2020.

As a private group, people must request to join. Non-hijabi and non-Muslim women are allowed to join so long as they have a genuine interest in learning about the community. Men are not permitted.

People participate to connect with others around the treatment that hijabi women face. “Due to all these little incidents that accumulate at the back of your head, you don't feel like you fit in, and you don't feel like you belong anywhere,” she told us. Women participate because the group provides a sense of belonging and a place where they feel safe sharing their experiences.

## Action

Surviving Hijab is very active online, with members sharing political, fashion, religious, and motivational content. The group has organized around specific causes related to the hijab.

For instance, when members reported that hotels and resorts across the Middle East were discriminating against women who wore the [burkini](https://www.thenational.ae/lifestyle/fashion/the-rise-of-the-burkini-how-the-modest-swimwear-has-gone-global-1.921794) - a hijab-compliant women’s swimsuit - other members began to call out those establishments on their Facebook and Instagram pages using #NoBurkiniBans and #NoHijabBans. Rostom says a few resorts and hotels reversed their burkini bans as a result of the campaign.

Surviving Hijab has also held meetups in real life. In July 2019, for instance, they [held an event](https://egyptianstreets.com/2019/07/07/womens-rights-movement-surviving-hijab-organizes-first-event-in-cairo/) at Greek Campus (an event space in downtown Cairo) with panel discussions, workshops, and beauty/makeup tips for group members.

## Challenges

As such a large group, Surviving Hijab often experiences interpersonal conflict. “When an argument breaks out, it’s hell,” Rostom told us. Rostom says that a common dispute starts when a member of the group posts a picture to show off her outfit, and has the fringe of her hair or her ankle exposed. Another member will call her out, saying her outfit does not count as hijab. Moderators try to catch these comments as soon as they are posted, to prevent the argument from escalating. “If I let the comment stay for more than five minutes, then it will just turn into a fire,” Rostom says.

For this reason, the group takes a tough stand on rule breaches. Moderators remove anyone who posts “this is not hijab” comments, as well as anyone who “likes” them (and is assumed to share those views). “It’s like a ‘bad apples’ theory,” Rostom explains. “If you leave one bad apple, it’s just going to ruin the whole group.”

Some members have also expressed frustration about the group’s focus on fashion, which they feel overshadows the goal of empowering women to succeed in other areas, such as their career. One member posted a comment that while clothing and modesty are important topics, the group needs to be more focused on highlighting certain aspects of their lives as hijabi women.[3]

These criticisms sometimes become overwhelming. Rostom says that members of the group are attacked both by stricter members of the community and by outside critics, who [stereotype](https://www.adl.org/education/resources/tools-and-strategies/myths-and-facts-about-muslim-people-and-islam) them as old-fashioned, extremist, or uneducated. “We have sad stories of women who left the group because it was too much for them,” Rostom says. “Or somebody annoyed them or that one hurtful comment left a scar and they couldn't get over it and then they ended up taking off the hijab.”

## Future Prospects

One of Rostom’s priorities is to make the group more financially sustainable. Surviving Hijab currently runs advertisements, mainly on its Instagram page, to raise money to pay the group’s moderation team. However, Rostom says that group leaders are often asked by Facebook and third parties to participate in interviews, events, and media appearances, which occupies a lot of their time without compensation.

In 2018, Surviving Hijab [won a USD $50,000 grant](https://darpanmagazine.com/people/newsmakers/manal-rostom-the-surviving-hijab-story/#:~:text=Later%20in%202018%2C%20Rostom%20won,efficiently%20through%20the%20required%20resources.) through the [Facebook Community Leadership Program](https://communities.fb.com/). However, Rostom says that processing the grant also brought a lot of work that was difficult for the group to handle. “As beautiful as it was, it was so stressful,” Rostom told us. “We did a lot of projects, and it grew our community, but where will this take us?” She would like to see some sort of retainer program or advertising credits to compensate leaders for the work they do with the group on a daily basis in order to make running the group more sustainable.

## Outcome and Impact

Surviving Hijab’s greatest impact has been helping its members to weather the personal challenges that come with being a woman who wears the hijab. Members report that the group has empowered them to take a stand against workplace discrimination. Others say they were considering taking off the hijab, but discovering Surviving Hijab inspired them to continue wearing it. “For us, for our religion and culture, to help women at that level is huge,” Rostom says.

Other women have contacted Rostom and said that her leadership has inspired their daughters to continue playing sports. “Representation matters,” Rostom told us, “and showcasing my story to these little kids will help them feel the freedom of being whoever they want to be.”

## Lessons learned

- **Remember the group’s purpose** \- The sensitive subject matter of Surviving Hijab has made the group a target of criticism. As the group’s public face, Rostom says she is often criticized for the decisions she makes, while also dealing with her own struggles over being a hijabi woman. She says she presses onward because she remembers what the group means in her life and in the lives of its other members. “I can shut down the group anytime I want, right?” she said. “...but  I will never do that because Surviving Hijab is my baby. The women hold on to this group like it’s their life sometimes.”
- **Set rules and stick to them** \- Running an online group gives Surviving Hijab’s moderators the ability to control the group’s activities and conversations in a way that would not be possible offline. Rostom points to the quick and consistent enforcement of the group’s rules against members who are judgemental or hateful. “The sense of security that we offer online is the option to immediately block and delete these haters - I don't think this exists and will ever exist offline,” Rostom told us. “In traditional communities there will always be this toxic group who's just trying to pull  the group down, but I feel like with online we have a lot more control.”

## End notes

1. Please note that “hijab” [can refer](https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/24118241) both to the dress code that many Muslim women follow as well as a type of headscarf used to comply with this dress code. Both meanings of the word are used throughout this case study.
2. Comment posted on September 30, 2020.

id: "virtual-communities:case/white-people-doing-something"
type: "GovLab case study"
title: "White People. DOING Something."
url: "https://virtual-communities.thegovlab.org/case/white-people-doing-something"
date: "2021-02-23"
summary: "Building a racial justice community around compassion and empathy"
source: "The GovLab (virtual-communities.thegovlab.org)"
licence: "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)"
